title: A Mixed-Method Assessment of Environmental Accessibility in Canadian Office Spaces: A Triangulation of IAQ Testing, Occupant Health Surveys, Scent-Free Policy Implementation, and Lived Experience
content: With individuals spending approximately 90% of their time indoors, indoor air quality (IAQ) is a critical public health and environmental accessibility concern. Fragranced consumer products emit volatile organic compounds (VOCs), potentially creating barriers for individuals with multiple chemical sensitivity (MCS) and other health vulnerabilities. This convergent mixed-methods study integrated five evidence streams: IAQ measurements, occupant surveys, scent-free policy assessments, product emissions testing, and focus groups to examine chemical exposures and environmental accessibility in Canadian offices. Findings indicated substantial contributions from indoor VOC sources. Despite greater mechanical ventilation, non-scent-free environments exhibited higher VOC concentrations and indoor/outdoor ratios, emphasizing source control alongside ventilation. Scent-free environments generally had lower VOC concentrations, although residual exposures persisted. Overlapping VOCs detected in indoor air and consumer products, alongside policy implementation gaps, highlighted ongoing exposure prevention challenges. Occupants of scent-free workplaces reported more symptoms and chronic conditions, potentially reflecting greater reliance on these environments among vulnerable individuals. Focus-group findings further identified persistent accessibility barriers and challenges with policy implementation. Overall, findings support integrated strategies combining scent-free policies, low-emission product procurement, transparent labelling, effective source control, adequate ventilation, and consistent implementation to reduce chemical exposures and advance environmental accessibility in workplaces.
